en: The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Zun pō xū mì jīng) states the essential summary of various sūtras: if a meal is offered for the deceased and the monastic community has distributed the food throughout, one then offers the food to the deceased;
if this is not done, the deceased will be unable to eat it.
Regarding the hells mentioned in the Sūtra:
if one leaves food for sentient beings before the meal has been distributed throughout the household where the fast is being observed,
that person enters the Hell of Severed Tongues.
The *Sūtra on the Determination of Sin and Merit* states:
"The discourse of Kātyāyana says that those who share two vows in one place [are linked]."
It is said that those who die become two-headed snakes that instruct one another.
The *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* states that not even a single grain or a single morsel from the Buddha’s plate at a layperson's offering feast is permitted for a worldly person.
One who eats food [in this manner] will receive the retribution of a hungry ghost (preta).
It is also said that [the food] is shared with insects and birds for them to eat.
The *Buddhaviṣayāvatāra-sūtra* states:
"If a person eats food from the alms bowl of the noble Saṃgha,
they incur immeasurable sin."
It is also said:
"It is shared with the guardians of the monastery, as well as with insects and birds.
This is stated in the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā-sūtra*.
In the case of a household observing the fast, regardless of its wealth,
one must not eat from the Buddha’s alms-bowl.
The presiding elder (upādhyāya) should manage the situation according to the Dharma.
If one does not do so, one incurs immeasurable sin. Question: Is it permissible to ransom [the victim] by paying a price?
According to the *Jueding zui fu jing* (Sūtra on the Determination of Sin and Merit), it is permitted.
Furthermore, because the Buddha did not seek out specific rules, there was no one capable [of establishing them].
The Elder taught that if one offers [the food] to the Buddha and the Sangha before partaking, one will be free from transgression.
If one does not do so, they will fall into the great hells for thousands or tens of thousands of kalpas.
If the teacher fails to instruct them, they too shall incur the same calamity;
even if they subsequently obtain a human body, they will remain among the lowly and base for nine million years.
Sheng said: "The Tripitaka states:
'It would be better to burn nine hundred oxen in a single day than to speak of the faults of the Triple Gem or one's preceptors and monks.'"
The transgression is grave.
According to the Ratnakūṭa Sūtra, there is no passing over it unharmed;
briefly stated, there are seven [cases].
The factors conducive to enlightenment are also called the Seven Jewels Spring,
and are also called the Seven Noble Treasures.
This is the account of how the frog attained rebirth in heaven through hearing the Dharma.
Excerpts from the Essential Summary of the *Sudarsana-vinaya-vibhāṣā*.
Formerly, when the Buddha was in the world, he arrived at the banks of Lake Kālaka in the kingdom of Campā and preached the Dharma for the assembly.
In that pond there was a frog who,
hearing the sound of the Buddha preaching the Dharma by the side of the pool,
immediately emerged from the water and went beneath the roots of a grass plant to listen to the Buddha’s teaching.
At that time, there was a man tending cattle with a staff who saw the Buddha seated there preaching the Dharma to the assembly.
Desiring to listen to the teaching, he went toward the Buddha and thrust his staff into the ground.
By mistakenly wearing a clam-shell headpiece,
he immediately ended his life and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
by virtue of his meritorious retribution, his palace measured twelve yojanas in length and breadth.
He enjoyed pleasures together with the celestial maidens.
Having been born in heaven, he attained the fruit of *srotāpanna* for the sake of hearing the Dharma.
A bird heard the bhikṣu reciting the sūtra and thereby gained the causal conditions for rebirth in heaven.
From the *Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish*: Long ago, when the Buddha was in the world, there was a bhikṣu reciting a sutra in a forest.
His voice was elegant and beautiful.
A bird heard the Dharma.
While he was listening beneath the tree,
he was struck by a hunter's arrow;
his life ended, and he was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Her countenance was upright and peerless;
she possessed the knowledge of her own past lives and knew that it was because she had seen a bhikṣu, read the sūtras, and listened to the Dharma that she had been born here.
He then took the celestial flowers and went to where the bhikṣu was;
he paid his respects, inquired after his well-being,
and offered the fragrant celestial flowers as an offering to the bhikṣu.
The bhikṣu questioned him and learned the details of the matter;
he then invited him to sit and preached the Dharma for him, whereby he attained the fruit of srotāpanna.
Having attained this fruit, he returned to the heavens.
If even birds and beasts who listen to the Dharma obtain immeasurable and boundless retribution from their past lives,
how much more so for humans who listen to the Dharma with faith— how could they not possess roots of goodness?
It is recorded that a parrot attained the condition of rebirth in heaven upon hearing the exposition of the Four Noble Truths.
From the *Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish*:
Formerly, when the Buddha was in the world,
there was an elder named Śreṣṭhin in the kingdom of Śrāvastī who had faith and reverence for the Buddha-dharma.
He provided everything necessary for the Saṃgha, the donors, and the assembly of monks.
In the house of Sudatta, there were two parrots;
one was named Lūka.
The second was named Śalati.
By nature he was clever and wise, and he understood the speech of others.
When the bhikṣu saw him coming, he first informed the household, instructing them to go out to receive and welcome him.
At a later time, Ānanda went to the house of the elder and saw that the bird was intelligent;
he preached the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—to it.
There was a tree in front of the gate.
The two birds, having heard the Dharma, flew toward the tree;
they joyfully recited and upheld it, and while staying overnight in the tree, they were eaten by a wild cat.
By virtue of these roots of goodness, they were reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and other such realms.
Having thus completed seven cycles of rebirth in the heavens,
he was born among humans, where he left the household life to practice the Way and attained the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha;
one was named Dharma.
The second is named Xiutandamo (Śuddhamā).
I have carefully examined the sūtras of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna;
it is stated therein that eating the *huqiu* (kṣāra) vegetable results in retribution in the evil destinies.
The *Dàshùn jīng* (Sūtra of Great Accordance) states:
"Those who eat this vegetable shall not hear the sūtras or the Buddha-dharma in their future births.
The *Huābào jīng* (Sūtra of Karmic Retribution) states:
Those who eat this vegetable will, in every place where they are born, fail to behold the Buddhas and will be afflicted by the eight types of increased maladies.
The Tianpan jing (Sūtra of the Heavenly Border) states:
"If one inadvertently eats this vegetable and does not feel regret, [the consequences will follow]."
One will dwell in the Avīci Hell for long kalpas with no prospect of escape.
If one intentionally consumes [forbidden food], there is no opportunity for repentance.
The Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra states:
This vegetable was produced when the celestial Māra Pāpīyān transformed his body into a thousand-year-old seductive fox; it grew where the fox had urinated.
One who eats this can destroy the Way.
Even if one does not encounter the various scriptures in this life, one will certainly do so in a future life.
Those who can become icchantikas of external paths by reviling the holy teachings,
and those whose worldly sins reach their ultimate limit through the five heinous crimes or stealing the property of the Sangha—
these cases do not admit of repentance.
If it is those who consume hempseed (huqiu) who commit the five heinous crimes or steal the property of the Sangha, I am indeed able to save them.
However, for those who consume hempseed vegetables whose own karma is profoundly heavy, even I cannot save them.
This refers to the onions and leeks mentioned in the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*.
Those who eat them incur the karmic offense of *saṃyojana*.
As the *Nāgārjuna-śāstra* states:

If a person who has eaten *huqiu* enters a Buddhist stūpa, they will fall into the Great Hell and undergo extreme suffering for a full ten kalpas as its primary retribution; furthermore, as its secondary retribution,
they shall dwell amidst foul excrement for immeasurable kalpas.
The *Pañcavidyā-śāstra* states:
"Those who eat this vegetable will become distracted and lose their right concentration;
spirits and deities will find an opportunity to harm them, and they will mostly fall into the Avīci Hell."
The Venerable Vasumitra recognized the words of his disciple, Bhramara, and said:
"You ought to protect the True Dharma and lead all sentient beings;
only by ensuring that the lineage of the Buddha is not severed can one truly be called a renunciant."
You should apply yourself with diligent vigor.
In the future, by abstaining from food, the five pungent roots (*gandha*), alcohol, and meat,
the ten grave precepts will naturally become pure, and you shall realize the fruits of the path in this very life.
If a person eats the *huqiu* (hemp) vegetable,
even if they are fully observant of the fast and precepts, upon death they will fall into the realm of the latrine-keepers;
this is decreed by the divine ordinances of merit.
I urge the Sangha to maintain the sacred precincts with secular decorum; do not eat *huqiu* (wild onions/garlic), lest you offend the Buddha’s countenance.
When a *sattva* leaps from a cliff, he must rely on his own discernment; what difficulty is there in choosing between vegetables?
Thus one cultivates the four right efforts.
First, one employs skillful means to prevent unarisen unwholesome states from arising;
second, one employs skillful means to eliminate unwholesome states that have already arisen;
third, one employs skillful means to bring about the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen.
Having given rise to the four wholesome dharmas, one employs skillful means to cause them to increase.
Evil issues from the mind and returns to the mind for its cessation;
goodness arises from the mind and returns to the mind for its growth.
One should diligently observe these four dharmas and cultivate the four immeasurable minds.
First, cultivate a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
To mind all sentient beings with the desire to grant them happiness;
to contemplate and provide immeasurable clothing, food, and other necessities to sentient beings, treating enemies and kin with equality;
and to cause them all to dwell in peace—this is called the cultivation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Second is the cultivation of compassion:
to keep in mind all sentient beings with the desire to uproot their suffering;
this is called the cultivation of compassion.
Third, cultivate a mind of sympathetic joy.
Contemplate all sentient beings:
if they cultivate goodness, I shall praise their goodness in its entirety.
If one encounters those who commit evil, one should encourage them to abandon it;
if one encounters those who do evil, one should extol the good.
Fourth, cultivate the mind of equanimity.
Regarding all sentient beings, one views them with complete equanimity, perceiving neither enemy nor friend;
they are identical to the dharma of emptiness.
One thus cultivates the six subtle practices.

First, consciousness does not bind itself to the contemplation of forms, nor is it defiled by attachment; the eye’s sublime conduct is clarity. Second, the ear does not cling to sounds—whether blue, yellow, crimson, or white.
Third, the nose is not stained by fragrances.
Fourth, the tongue does not savor flavors.
Fifth, the body does not cling to smoothness and so forth.
Sixth, the mind does not contemplate unwholesome dharmas.
Regarding the four debts of gratitude:
first is the debt to one's parents,
who were able to give birth to one's own body and enable one to exist today.
Second is the debt of gratitude to one's preceptors,
who give birth to one's Dharma-body by bestowing the gift of the Dharma upon me.
Third is the debt of gratitude to kings.
The earth, water, trees, and grasses constantly provide for me;
this is the kindness of the four donors who supply me with clothing and food to sustain my life.
There are four classes of donors (*dānapati*):
first, the class of devas, who offer ambrosia from celestial kitchens to those who have left the household life;
second, the class of nāgas, who offer milk to oxen, deer, and monkeys.
